title: Client Intake and Triage
answer: Client intake and triage is the front end of legal service delivery, where a firm or legal department captures a new matter, checks for conflicts, and decides how it will be handled. It covers the first contact, the collection of client and matter details, and the routing of the request to the right person or queue. crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Client intake and triage is the front end of legal service delivery, where a firm or legal department captures a new matter, checks for conflicts, and decides how it will be handled. It covers the first contact, the collection of client and matter details, and the routing of the request to the right person or queue. In practice it sits between business development, risk, and the practice groups, and it is often the first place a legal team applies automation. The work is administrative at heart but it sets the record that everything downstream depends on.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Intake systems typically combine a web or email front end, a conflicts and parties database, a matter management or practice management platform, and a document store. Larger organisations connect these to billing, customer relationship management, and identity systems so that a new client or matter is created once and referenced everywhere. Security matters here because intake collects personal and sometimes privileged information, so access control, encryption, and audit logging are standard expectations. Many teams now place a language model or classification service in front of the form to read free text enquiries and extract the parties, the type of matter, and any urgency.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The usual pattern is to define the questions and the routing rules first, then automate the reading of unstructured enquiries. A model or rules engine classifies the matter type, flags conflicts against known parties, and scores urgency or value so that a human reviewer sees a shortlist rather than a raw inbox. Human review stays in the loop for anything ambiguous, conflicted, or high value, and the reviewer's decision is fed back to improve the rules. Teams measure cycle time from enquiry to assignment, the rate of misrouted matters, and the proportion of enquiries that need no manual touch. The output is a structured matter record plus a routing decision, not a legal opinion.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Intake touches client confidentiality, conflict of interest rules, and data protection, so the record of who saw what and when is part of the compliance story. Firms need a lawful basis for the personal data they collect, a retention schedule, and a clear path for a client to correct or remove information. Automated triage should be explainable enough that a reviewer can say why a matter was routed or declined, and any model used on client text should be covered by the firm's vendor and data handling terms.Nothing here is legal advice, and a firm should take its own view on conflicts and confidentiality obligations.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect intake to move from forms toward conversational capture, with a model drafting the matter summary and the conflict check from a short exchange. That shifts the human role toward review and exception handling, and it raises the bar on audit trails and on proving that a decline or a conflict flag was reasoned. Integration with matter management and billing will matter more than the model itself, because a good classification that never reaches the system of record saves little. The open questions are how firms evidence the basis of an automated routing decision and how they keep client text out of systems they cannot govern. Watch the compliance and case law pages on this site for how those questions get answered in practice.
